sections.h2: What is an Ohio transfer on death designation affidavit?
sections.html:
It is a sworn document that names who receives an Ohio home or other real estate when the owner dies, without a probate transfer of that parcel. The authority is Revised Code 5302.22, and the companion rules sit in sections 5302.222 and 5302.23.

The affidavit only works if it is recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies. It does not need a buyer's signature, a payment, or delivery to the person named. Ohio law also says that a transfer made this way is not testamentary, so it takes priority over a will or the intestacy rules for that property.

Owners sometimes mix this up with a transfer on death deed. Ohio's current statute calls the instrument an affidavit, and the older deed form is only mentioned for designations made before the 2009 change.

sections.h2: Who can sign the affidavit and what must it contain?
sections.html:
A sole owner, a tenant in common, or a survivorship tenant can sign, and a married owner signs together with the spouse. The owner may designate the whole interest or only a stated part of it.

The affidavit has to be verified before a person who can administer oaths. Under 5302.22(D) it must include:

  • A description of the real property and a reference to a recorded instrument that contains the description.
  • If less than the full interest is passing, a statement of the specific part.
  • A statement that the signer appears on the record as owner when the affidavit is recorded, plus the owner's marital status.
  • For a married owner, a statement from the spouse that dower rights are subordinate to the beneficiary's title.
  • At least one beneficiary identified by name.

Anyone who knowingly lies in the affidavit commits falsification under division (A)(6) of section 2921.13. The county recorder cannot draft the document for you, so people usually have an attorney or a title company prepare it.

sections.h2: How is the affidavit recorded, and what does it cost?
sections.html:
You offer it to the recorder of the county where the land sits, and the recorder records it the same way a deed is recorded and charges the deed fee. The recorder indexes it under the name of the owner who signed.

The fee schedule in section 317.32 splits each charge into a base fee and a housing trust fund fee. A county may also add a document preservation surcharge of up to $5, so the final total depends on the county. Ask the recorder for the all-in figure before you mail a check.

Some recorders add to the process. The Pickaway County recorder, for example, says on its recording page that a transfer on death designation cannot be sent by mail because it needs the auditor and engineer stamps first, so it has to be walked through in person.

sections.h2: Does the affidavit change who owns the house while the owner is alive?
sections.html:
No. Section 5302.23 says the designation has no effect on present ownership, and the named beneficiary has no interest in the property until the owner dies. The owner can still sell, mortgage, lease or live in the house.

That matters if you plan to sell. A buyer's title company will see the recorded affidavit in the chain of title, but the owner can convey the property by deed without the beneficiary's consent. Once a deed to a buyer is recorded, the affidavit has nothing left to act on.

The designation also does nothing to lien holders. A mortgagee, judgment creditor or mechanic's lien holder keeps every right it had, and it does not have to name the beneficiary in a foreclosure unless that person holds some other interest in the land.

sections.h2: Can the owner change or revoke the designation?
sections.html:
Yes, at any time and without the beneficiary's consent. The owner records a new transfer on death designation affidavit that states the change, and a later-recorded affidavit supersedes every earlier recorded one for that property.

The statute also builds in several automatic effects:

  • If a named beneficiary dies first and a contingent beneficiary was named, the contingent person takes the same share.
  • If no named beneficiary survives and none is contingent, the interest falls into the owner's probate estate.
  • Several beneficiaries take equal shares as tenants in common unless the affidavit says otherwise or makes them survivorship tenants.
  • If the owner's spouse is the beneficiary and the marriage later ends by divorce, dissolution or annulment, the spouse is treated as having died before the owner.

A recorded affidavit also bars dower rights from vesting in a spouse the owner marries afterward, unless the designation is changed or revoked.

sections.h2: What does the beneficiary do after the owner dies?
sections.html:
The beneficiary records an affidavit of confirmation. Under section 5302.222, the transfer is recorded by presenting it to the county auditor of the county and filing it with the county recorder. It must be verified before a person who can administer oaths and must come with a certified copy of the owner's death certificate.

The affidavit of confirmation has to give the name and address of each surviving beneficiary, the date of death, a description of the property, and the name of any beneficiary who did not survive. A certified death certificate is also required for each beneficiary who died before the owner.

If the title is registered land under Chapter 5309, a different procedure applies, found in section 5309.081. The beneficiary takes only what the owner held on the date of death, including any mortgage, reservation or exception that was already on the property.

sections.h2: Is there a conveyance fee on a transfer on death transfer?
sections.html:
Often not, but the auditor decides on the form. Section 319.54(G)(3) lists transfers that do not carry the auditor's fee, including a transfer where no money or other valuable consideration is paid and the transaction is not a gift. When an exemption applies, section 319.202 says the statement filed with the auditor only has to give the reason for the exemption.

Auditors use the state's DTE 100 family of forms for this. The Paulding County auditor says form DTE 100 (EX) is needed when claiming an exemption, and Pickaway County will not transfer an instrument without a completed DTE 100 or DTE 100EX. Ask your own auditor which form it wants with an affidavit of confirmation.

The recording fee at the recorder's counter is separate from any auditor charge and follows the same schedule as a deed.

sections.h2: Can a house with a recorded affidavit still be sold quickly?
sections.html:
Yes, while the owner is alive, the owner signs the deed and the sale closes like any other. After the owner's death, the beneficiary must first record the affidavit of confirmation, and only then can a deed to a buyer move through the auditor and recorder.

Beneficiaries who inherit this way avoid opening an estate for that parcel, which often saves weeks. They still have to deal with the mortgage balance, unpaid property tax, repairs and any co-owners, because the beneficiary takes the property subject to everything recorded against it.

If you inherited an Ohio house this way and want to sell it as-is for cash, a recorded affidavit of confirmation is the document a buyer will ask for first.

faqs.q: Does a transfer on death affidavit avoid probate in Ohio?
faqs.a: For the parcel it covers, yes. Under Revised Code 5302.23 the transfer is not testamentary and overrides a will or intestate transfer of that property. If no named or contingent beneficiary survives, the property goes into the owner's probate estate.

faqs.q: Must the beneficiary sign the affidavit?
faqs.a: No. Section 5302.22(F) says the affidavit needs no consideration and does not have to be delivered to the beneficiary. It becomes effective only when recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies.

faqs.q: Can an owner name a trust as beneficiary?
faqs.a: Yes. A beneficiary can be a natural or legal person, including a bank acting as trustee of a trust. If the trustee is replaced by a successor before the owner's death, the successor trustee counts as the beneficiary, and the affidavit of confirmation must name that successor.

faqs.q: What if the owner was married when the affidavit was signed?
faqs.a: The spouse signs with the owner, and the spouse's dower rights become subordinate to the beneficiary's title. If the spouse is named beneficiary and the couple later divorces, dissolves the marriage or has it annulled, the designation of the spouse ends.

faqs.q: Does a recorded affidavit stop a lender from foreclosing?
faqs.a: No. Lien holders keep all of their rights, and the beneficiary takes the property subject to existing encumbrances. A foreclosing lender does not have to join the beneficiary unless that person holds another interest in the land.
